chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu Hamza, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Whichever believer visits a sick believer, he plunges into divine mercy with a deep plunging. So when he sits, the mercy overwhelms him. So when he departs, God assigns seventy thousand angels to be with him, seeking forgiveness for him and seeking mercy for him, and they say: 'You have done good, and Paradise has been made good for you' up to that very hour the next day.

And there would be for him, O Abu Hamza, a kharif in Paradise. I said: And what is the kharif, may I be your ransom? He said: A vast expanse in Paradise that a rider would travel in it for forty years.

key_terms.الخريف: Kharif — an untranslatable term explained by the Imam as a vast corner or expanse in Paradise traversable only over forty years on horseback
key_terms.الرحمة: Divine mercy (rahmah) — the grace and compassion of God that envelops righteous acts
key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: A term of deep reverence meaning 'may I be sacrificed for you', used by companions when addressing the Imams
key_terms.عاد: Visited the sick (عيادة المريض, 'iyada al-marid) — the Islamic practice of visiting the ill

ai.seo_question: What is the reward for visiting a sick Muslim in Islam according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) describes the immense spiritual reward for visiting a sick fellow believer. The visitor is enveloped in divine mercy, accompanied by seventy thousand angels who pray for his forgiveness until the same hour the following day, and he is granted a vast portion of Paradise called a 'kharif' — an expanse so large that a mounted rider would take forty years to traverse it. This teaching reflects the Shia emphasis on fulfilling the rights of fellow believers (huquq al-mu'minin) as a means of drawing near to God and earning paradise.
